title: Cookbook:Daifuku (Sweet Filled Mochi)
steps: Prepare anko filling as directed. Shape into 12 small, marble-sized balls and set aside.
Prepare a smooth surface, such as a cutting board, by coating with potato starch; be generous, as the dough will be very sticky.

Heat water and sugar together in a microwave until sugar is dissolved. Add rice flour and stir completely. Microwave for 2 minutes, remove and stir. Microwave for 2 more minutes, or until dough begins to expand. Remove from microwave, stir again, and remove the dough to the potato starch-coated surface. The dough, called mochi, will be very hot.
Spread or roll the mochi dough out until thin. Using a knife, cut into 12 even sized pieces.
Coat the palms and fingers of your hands in potato starch. Spread each piece out as thin as possible.
Place an anko ball in the middle of each mochi piece, then wrap the mochi around the ball, forming a bigger ball.
Roll shaped daifuku in potato starch, and set on a plate dusted with potato starch or a piece of wax paper.
Serve warm or cool. Store in an airtight container. Very perishable.
description: Daifukumochi (大福餅), or Daifuku (大福) (literally "great luck"), is a Japanese confection consisting of a small round mochi (glutinous rice cake) stuffed with sweet filling, most commonly anko, sweetened red bean paste made from azuki beans.

Forming: 20 minutes|difficulty=2 | Image = [[Image:Soft-rice-cake-stuffed-with-sweetened-bean-jam,daifuku,katori-city,japan.JPG|300px]] }} {{Recipe}} '''Daifukumochi (大福餅)''', or '''Daifuku (大福)''' (literally "great luck"), is a Japanese [[Cookbook:Confections|confection]] consisting of a small round ''mochi'' (glutinous rice cake) stuffed with sweet filling, most commonly ''[[Cookbook:Red Bean Paste|anko]]'', sweetened red bean paste made from azuki beans. Daifuku comes in many varieties. The most common is white, pale green or pale pink colored mochi filled with anko. These come in two sizes, one approximately the diameter of a half-dollar coin, the other palm-sized. Some versions contain whole pieces of fruit, mixtures of fruit and anko or crushed melon paste. Nearly all daifuku are covered in a fine layer of potato or taro starch to keep them from sticking to each other, or to the fingers. Some are covered with confectioner's sugar or cocoa. ==Ingredients== *[[Cookbook:Red Bean Paste|Anko filling]] *~½ cup [[Cookbook:Potato Starch|potato starch]] (''katakuriko'') *1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] sweet glutinous [[Cookbook:Rice Flour|rice flour]] (''mochiko'') *⅔ cup [[Cookbook:Water|water]] *¼ cup white granulated [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]] ==Procedure== # Prepare [[Cookbook:Red Bean Paste|anko filling]] as directed. Shape into 12 small, marble-sized balls and set aside. # Prepare a smooth surface, such as a [[Cookbook:Cutting Board|cutting board]], by coating with potato starch; be generous, as the dough will be very sticky. # Heat water and sugar together in a [[Cookbook:Microwave|microwave]] until sugar is dissolved. Add rice flour and stir completely. Microwave for 2 minutes, remove and stir. Microwave for 2 more minutes, or until dough begins to expand. Remove from microwave, stir again, and remove the dough to the potato starch-coated surface. The dough, called ''[[Cookbook:Mochi|mochi]]'', will be very hot. # Spread or [[Cookbook:Dough#Rolling|roll]] the mochi dough out until thin. Using a [[Cookbook:Knife|knife]], cut into 12 even sized pieces. # Coat the palms and fingers of your hands in potato starch. Spread each piece out as thin as possible. # Place an anko ball in the middle of each mochi piece, then wrap the mochi around the ball, forming a bigger ball. # Roll shaped daifuku in potato starch, and set on a plate dusted with potato starch or a piece of wax paper. # Serve warm or cool. Store in an airtight container. Very perishable. ==Notes, tips, and variations== *Chocolate [[Cookbook:Ganache|ganache]] may be substituted for anko paste. *[[Cookbook:Food Coloring|Food coloring]] may be added to the water before the rice flour is mixed in. *[[Cookbook:Cocoa powder|Cocoa powder]] may be used instead of potato starch in the final step.
